effect_estimate.comment: Outcome 'infrastructure access' is the average of district-level percentages of households with protected water and protected sanitation (BPS/SUSENAS). Comparing newly created districts to split districts alone yields statistically insignificant estimates, whereas comparing newly created districts to all original districts shows a statistically significant negative impact starting in the second year of operations, attributed in exploratory comparisons to weaker governance and procurement corruption in new jurisdictions.
effect_estimate.value: Relative to original districts (336 districts), new local government creation via district splitting had no contemporaneous effect on household protected water and sanitation access (static DiD FE: -0.027 percentage points, SE = 0.649; dynamic difference-GMM: 0.104 percentage points, SE = 0.593) but significantly reduced access in the second year of operations (lagged new district) by -0.987 percentage points (SE = 0.579, p < .10; N = 2,714) in the static FE model and by -1.351 percentage points (SE = 0.584, p < .05; N = 2,693) in the dynamic difference-GMM model, implying a long-run reduction of approximately -1.75 percentage points (= -1.35 / (1 - 0.23), p = .023). Relative to split districts alone (98 districts), effects on water and sanitation access were not statistically significant (static FE lagged: -0.923, SE = 0.726, N = 750; dynamic GMM lagged: -0.690, SE = 0.769, N = 733). In exploratory governance comparisons, new districts had higher parliamentary political fragmentation (6.67 vs. 5.77 effective parties, p < .01) and lower BPK financial audit scores (1.31 vs. 1.74 on a 0-3 scale, p < .01) than original districts.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF pp. 10-11, Section 'Impact of district splitting on service access', Tables 4-5; PDF pp. 12-13, Section 'Underlying causal mechanisms', Table 7

mechanism_certainty.comment: Quasi-experimental panel DiD and dynamic difference-GMM design appraised with ROBINS-I at Moderate overall risk of bias (districts collapsed to constant 2001 boundaries, district and year fixed effects, district-specific linear time trends in static model, lagged outcome instrumentation passing Hansen p = .439 and weak-instrument CLR p = .001 tests in dynamic model, negative-binomial exogeneity test of split timing in Table A2, and insignificant 1- and 2-year pre-treatment leads in Table 6). Causal effect of administrative splitting (institutional_fragmentation) is rated 3; secondary governance/corruption proxy analysis (political fragmentation and BPK audit opinions) is explicitly exploratory and descriptive.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 9-13, Sections 'Methods', 'Impact of district splitting on service access', and 'Underlying causal mechanisms'; Tables 4-7, A2-A3

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines subnational administrative jurisdiction splitting/proliferation (pemekaran; institutional_fragmentation), national-local parliamentary coalitions bypassing Ministry of Home Affairs regulatory vetting and multiparty fragmentation in district legislatures (political_coordination), local executive/legislative discretion and elite capture in tendered public works contracting (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, discretion), and central moratoria plus Supreme Audit Agency (BPK) annual financial/regulatory compliance audits (ENFORCEMENT).
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 5-6, Section 'District splitting in Indonesia: Process and outcomes'; PDF pp. 11-14, Sections 'Underlying causal mechanisms' and 'Summary and conclusions', Table 7

outcome_flags.comment: Measures district-level percentage of households with access to protected water (piped water, communal tap, rainwater, spring water, covered wells) and protected sanitation (flush toilet, piped sewer, flush/pour-flush pit latrine, ventilated pit latrine), combined as an average district service access/coverage indicator. Author explicitly notes in Note 2 (PDF p. 15) that service quality is not studied due to lack of data.
outcome_flags.where_found: PDF p. 8, Section 'Data'; PDF p. 15, Notes 2 and 5

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Non-randomized quasi-experimental panel evaluation of administrative district splitting using static generalized difference-in-differences (with district FE, year FE, and district-specific time trends) and dynamic Arellano-Bond difference-GMM with never-split/original and not-yet-split district comparators; ROBINS-I is the matching tool per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1.
risk_of_bias_tool.where_found: PDF pp. 9-12, Sections 'Methods' and 'Impact of district splitting on service access', Tables 4-6

sample_size.comment: Districts are collapsed into constant 2001 boundaries for longitudinal panel estimation over 2001-2010; underlying household water and sanitation indicators are aggregated to the district-year level from BPS annual SUSENAS household surveys (individual household N not reported). Exogeneity test in Table A2 uses 92 split districts.
sample_size.value: 336 original districts (collapsed to 2001 boundaries over 2001-2010: 238 never-split districts and 98 split districts that formed 253 new districts [98 parent and 155 child], with 491 districts at end of 2010 and 589 total local governments operating during 2001-2010); Original vs. new regressions: 336 districts, 2,714 district-year observations (static FE) and 2,693 district-year observations (dynamic GMM infrastructure; 2,677 education); Split vs. new regressions: 98 districts, 750 district-year observations (static FE) and 733 district-year observations (dynamic GMM infrastructure; 725 education)
sample_size.where_found: PDF p. 6, Table 1; PDF p. 9, Table 3; PDF pp. 10-11, Tables 4-5; PDF p. 18, Table A1; PDF p. 19, Table A2

study_design.comment: Exploits plausibly exogenous timing of subnational administrative splits (including central government moratoria and parliamentary delays) across a 10-year district-year panel (2001-2010), supplemented with pre-trend lead falsification tests, negative binomial split-timing exogeneity regressions, and exploratory cross-group comparisons of governance proxies.
study_design.value: Quasi-experimental longitudinal district-level panel study (2001-2010) using static generalized difference-in-differences (two-way fixed effects with district-specific time trends) and dynamic Arellano-Bond difference-GMM estimation
study_design.where_found: PDF p. 2, Abstract; PDF pp. 9-10, Section 'Methods'; PDF pp. 11-12, Table 5 and Table 6
